title: Mizoram, India's Ginger Capital, Bets on GI-Tagged Crop for Export Markets
excerpt: NITI Aayog recognised Mizoram as the Ginger Capital of India in 2025. Behind the title sit GI-tagged Thingpui and Thinglaidum varieties with oleoresin at 6-8%, Rs 137.72 crore paid to farmers in 2025, and four new processing units planned in Champhai.
body:
• NITI Aayog recognised Mizoram as the 'Ginger Capital of India' in 2025, citing the state's high-quality ginger production and strong agricultural output.
  • Mizo ginger has held a Geographical Indication (GI) tag since 14 September 2021, and Ministry of DoNER figures cited by industry experts put its oleoresin content at 6-8%, against a stated global average of about 3%.
  • The Mizoram Agricultural Marketing Board procured over 3.38 crore kg of ginger in 2025 and disbursed the full support price of Rs 137.72 crore to farmers.
  • For shoppers, the label to look for is GI-tagged Mizo ginger - local varieties such as Thingpui and Thinglaidum - which records crude fibre of just 5.74% and is sought after for food processing, pharmaceutical and export use.

Mizoram has been officially recognised as the Ginger Capital of India by NITI Aayog, a title earned in 2025 for the quality and scale of its ginger output, according to an Indian Express explainer on the state's rise as India's ginger hub. For a crop central to Indian cooking and Ayurvedic practice alike, the designation puts a small hill state at the top of a national supply chain.

"Mizoram has begun to be known as the 'Ginger Capital of India'. This growing recognition is a result of the hard work of farmers."

— Lalduhoma, Chief Minister of Mizoram

What Makes Mizo Ginger Different

The case rests on chemistry as much as volume. Shilpa Agrawal, Vice President and Head of Operations at the Ind Food and Beverage Association (IFBA), describes Mizo ginger as a premium, GI-tagged product distinguished by high oleoresin content, strong pungency, low fibre and suitability for pharmaceutical, food-processing and export markets. The GI application documents locally cultivated varieties including Thingpui and Thinglaidum, with crude fibre content of 5.74%, gingerol content of approximately 1.25%, volatile oil content of 1.80% and dry matter content of 22.47%. A third local cultivar, Thingaria, is also recognised for its distinctive flavour profile.

Those numbers trace back to the land itself. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) identifies ginger as a significant cash crop in Mizoram's subtropical hill zone, characterised by acidic soils and annual rainfall of approximately 2,000-3,200 mm. The GI tag, registered on 14 September 2021, protects that geographical identity - and, as Agrawal notes, creates a route for farmers to access premium markets rather than selling an undifferentiated commodity.

The Procurement Numbers Behind the Title

The state's support system has put money behind the branding. As per the annual report of the Mizoram Agricultural Marketing Board (MAMB), over 3.38 crore kg of ginger was procured in 2025, and the entire support price amounting to Rs 137.72 crore has been fully disbursed to farmers, Chief Minister Lalduhoma said while inaugurating a ginger processing unit at the Sairang Horticulture Centre, around 21 km from Aizawl. Lalduhoma said ginger cultivation has enabled many families to earn better incomes, and he urged farmers to sell through collection centres so procurement stays systematic.

From Raw Rhizomes to Processed Exports

The next phase is value addition. Ginger has been identified as Mizoram's Unique Selling Proposition (USP) crop under the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER), and in June the state launched the Mizo Ginger USP Mission Projects alongside an export awareness workshop run with the National Cooperative Exports Limited (NCEL). Under a Sustainable Cultivation and Post-Harvest Management Project supported by DoNER, four modern ginger processing units are being established in Champhai district, Mizoram's largest ginger-producing district, with financial support of Rs 30.13 crore, according to IANS reporting in The Freedom Press. The initiative is expected to benefit around 20,000 ginger-growing households and generate about 100 jobs, with high-value products including ginger oil in development.

Lalduhoma has been explicit about the direction of travel: the state needs to move beyond selling raw ginger and focus on processing and value addition to raise farmers' income. While Mizoram ginger is smaller in size, he said, its exceptional quality and pharmaceutical-grade standards give it a strong competitive advantage in national and international markets.

What It Means in the Kitchen

For Indian households - in Mizoram, across India and in the diaspora - ginger is not a garnish but a foundation: grated into chai, ground into curry pastes, and used in home remedies. A low-fibre, high-oleoresin rhizome grinds smoother and delivers more pungency per gram, which is exactly the profile the GI documentation records for Thingpui and Thinglaidum. As processed Mizo products - dried ginger, extracts and ginger oil - reach shelves under the GI identity, diaspora shoppers buying for flavour rather than bulk have a specific origin to ask for by name. Whether the title converts into durable export income now depends on the Champhai units and the market linkages the state says it is building.
